Solve a Quadratic Assignment Problem

Source: R/qap.R
qap.Rd

Solve a quadratic assignment problem (QAP) with a simulated annealing or robust tabu search heuristic. qap.obj() calculates the objective value of an assignment.

Usage

qap(A, B, method = NULL, ...)

qap.obj(A, B, o)

Arguments

A

A numeric matrix of flows between facilities. For qap(), it must be at least 2 by 2, symmetric, nonnegative, and finite.

B

A numeric matrix of distances between locations. For qap(), it must have the same dimensions as A and be symmetric, nonnegative, and finite.

method

Solver name: "SA" (simulated annealing, the default) or "RoTS" (robust tabu search).

...

Additional arguments passed to the selected solver. See Details.

o

A permutation of 1:nrow(A) assigning facilities to locations.

Value

qap() returns an integer vector of facility to location assignments with the objective value in its "obj" attribute. qap.obj() returns the objective value for permutation o.

Details

The problem is to assign \(n\) facilities to \(n\) locations to minimize total transportation or interaction costs. Required flows between the facilities are represented by the matrix \(A\) and distances between locations is given in matrix \(B\). The QAP seeks an assignment that minimizes the sum of flows times distance. For an assignment represented by a \(n \times n\) permutation matrix \(X\) used to assign the facilities to the locations in the order given by the permutation, the objective can be written as

$$\min_{X \in \Pi}\; \mathrm{tr}(AXB^TX^T)$$

where \(\Pi\) is the set of all valid \(n \times n\) permutation matrices. Note that for symmetric distances, the distance matrix \(B\) does not need to be transposed.

The QAP originated as a facility location problem (Koopmans and Beckmann, 1957) and also has applications in data analysis (Hubert and Schultz, 1976). It is NP-hard. Two heuristics are available.

Simulated Annealing

method = "SA" uses the simulated annealing heuristic of Burkard and Rendl (1984), based on Rendl's Fortran implementation from QAPLIB. The authors suggest it can produce heuristic solutions for problems with up to 256 objects, although the implementation does not enforce this limit.

Additional arguments for method = "SA" are:

rep

Positive integer number of restarts. More restarts can help with local optima. Default: 1L.

miter

Positive integer number of iterations at a fixed temperature. Increasing miter typically leads to modest reduction in the optimality gap while increasing runtime. Default: 2 * nrow(A).

fiter

Factor of at least 1 by which miter grows after each cooling step. Larger values lead to very long runtimes. Default 1.1.

ft

Factor by which the temperature decreases after each cooling step. When increasing this value, maxsteps also needs to be increased. Default 0.5 (strictly between 0 and 1).

maxsteps

Positive integer maximum number of cooling steps. The search also stops earlier once it has frozen, i.e., the objective value did not change during a whole step. With the default cooling rate this typically happens for problems with less than 150 objects before the default maxsteps of 50 is reached, however, larger problems can benefit from increasing maxsteps. Default 50L.

verbose

Print the parameter settings and, for each restart, the best and current objective values, the number of cooling steps used, the final temperature, and the run time; default FALSE.

A good starting point for experiments is to set maxsteps very large (e.g., 100000) and then slow down cooling by increasing ft from 0.5 in 0.1 steps towards 1. Use verbose = TRUE to see the algorithm's behavior given the parameters and if maxsteps stop simulated annealing too early with a high final temperature.

Robust Tabu Search

method = "RoTS" uses the robust tabu search of Taillard (1991). It repeatedly moves to the best pairwise exchange of two facilities that is not tabu, where a tabu tenure that varies randomly around tenure iterations prevents facilities from returning to recently used locations. Moves are accepted regardless of tabu status if they give a new best solution or place a facility at a location it has not used for more than aspiration iterations. Random numbers come from R's generator, so results can be reproduced with set.seed().

Additional arguments for method = "RoTS" are:

rep

Positive integer number of restarts from random permutations. More restarts reduce the dependence on the starting permutation. Default 1L.

iter

Positive integer number of tabu search iterations per restart. The run time grows linearly with iter. Default 100 * nrow(A).

tenure

Positive integer mean tabu tenure. The actual tenure is drawn uniformly from 0.9 to 1.1 times this value. A longer tenure forbids more moves and pushes the search further away from the current region, a shorter tenure makes it more greedy. Default nrow(A).

aspiration

Nonnegative number of iterations after which an unused placement may override the tabu status. Default 5 * nrow(A)^2.

verbose

Print the parameter settings and, for each restart, the best and current objective values, the iteration at which the best solution was found (best_iter), the number of tabu moves taken because of aspiration (aspired), and the run time; default FALSE.

Unlike simulated annealing, tabu search always runs for iter iterations. The tabu tenure controls how strongly the search is pushed to explore and stays fixed during the run. The defaults follow Taillard (1991) and worked well for many small QAPLIB problems where small changes of the parameters tenure and aspiration often make very little difference.

Use verbose = TRUE to check best_iter: if the best solution is found close to iter, the search was still improving and iter should be increased. If it is found much earlier, the rest of the run added little, and a smaller iter with more restarts may be more effective.

References

Burkard, R. E. and Rendl, F. (1984). A thermodynamically motivated simulation procedure for combinatorial optimization problems. European Journal of Operational Research, 17(2), 169-174. doi:10.1016/0377-2217(84)90231-5

Koopmans, T. C. and Beckmann, M. (1957). Assignment problems and the location of economic activities. Econometrica, 25(1), 53-76. doi:10.2307/1907742

Taillard, E. (1991). Robust taboo search for the quadratic assignment problem. Parallel Computing, 17(4-5), 443-455. doi:10.1016/S0167-8191(05)80147-4

Hubert, L. and Schultz, J. (1976). Quadratic assignment as a general data analysis strategy. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 29(2), 190-241. doi:10.1111/j.2044-8317.1976.tb00714.x

See also

read_qaplib()

Examples

set.seed(1234)
p <- read_qaplib(system.file("qaplib", "had12.dat", package = "qap"))
cat("Optimal solution:", p$opt)
#> Optimal solution: 1652

a <- qap(p$A, p$B, verbose = TRUE, rep = 5)
#> Simulated annealing heuristic by Burkard and Rendl.
#> Parameters: n = 12, rep = 5, miter = 24, fiter = 1.1, ft = 0.5, maxsteps = 50
#>   rep   best_obj  current_obj  steps   final_temp     time
#>     1       1684         1684     11        1.844   0.000s
#>     2       1678         1678     12        0.922   0.000s
#>     3       1660         1660     12        0.922   0.000s
#>     4       1654         1654     12        0.922   0.000s
#>     5       1654         1696     11        1.844   0.000s
a
#>  [1]  8 10  2 11 12  5  6  7  3  1  4  9
#> attr(,"obj")
#> [1] 1654
cat("optimality gap:", (attr(a, "obj") - p$opt) / p$opt * 100, "%")
#> optimality gap: 0.1210654 %

# robust tabu search often finds the optimal solution
a <- qap(p$A, p$B, method = "RoTS", rep = 5, verbose = TRUE)
#> Robust tabu search by Taillard.
#> Parameters: n = 12, rep = 5, iter = 1200, tenure = 12, aspiration = 720
#>   rep   best_obj  current_obj  best_iter   aspired     time
#>     1       1652         1652         26         1   0.001s
#>     2       1652         1660         89         2   0.001s
#>     3       1652         1652        837         3   0.001s
#>     4       1652         1652         12         0   0.000s
#>     5       1652         1652         45         3   0.001s
a
#>  [1]  3 10 11  2 12  5  6  7  8  1  4  9
#> attr(,"obj")
#> [1] 1652
cat("optimality gap:", (attr(a, "obj") - p$opt) / p$opt * 100, "%")
#> optimality gap: 0 %
